2.text: herself with a wooden knife. But, on seeing the peltries, nobody would even

3.text: look at the tricks of the shaman-woman, and she, in her turn, was expelled.¹

4.text: Similar practices existed among the Yukaghir. Thus, for instance, in the

5.text: village Pyatistennoye I found, together with the wooden painted plank before

6.text: mentioned,² drums, shamanistic dress, and other appurtenances of the shamanistic

7.text: practice. Among other things was an old wooden knife covered with dark

8.text: spots, which were said by the natives to be the shaman’s blood, which flowed

9.text: down when he stabbed himself through the abdomen.

10.text: Krasheninnikoff describes a Kamchadal shaman, who likewise stabbed

11.text: himself with a knife while having the fur shirt on, and then drew from under

12.text: its cover handfuls of blood, which he swallowed.³

13.text: Sarytcheff tells the same of a Yakut shaman, who not only stabbed

14.text: himself through the abdomen, but even ordered his assistant to drive in the

15.text: knife with a log up to the handle. After that the shaman came to the

16.text: hearth, took three burning coals, and swallowed them with much composure

18.text: To describe any considerable number of tricks carried out by the shamans,

19.text: both Chukchee and Eskimo, would require too much space. Uˊpuñe, for

20.text: instance, pretended to draw a cord through her body, passing it from one

21.text: spot to another. Then suddenly she drew it out, and immediately afterward

22.text: pretended to cut in two with it the bodies of several of her children, who

23.text: sat in front of her. These and other tricks resemble to a surprising degree

24.text: the feats of jugglers all over the world. Before each performance, Uˊpuñe

25.text: would even open her hands, in the graceful manner of a professor of magic,

26.text: to show us that she had nothing in them.

27.text: It was said that her deceased husband had been able to wander under-

28.text: ground with his drum and all, that is, to “sink” in a quite literal manner.

29.text: During a séance in the dark, he would require two of his neighbors to put

30.text: their hands upon his head, then he would gradually sink into the earth until

31.text: they lost the last touch of his hair. After a while, some one would be heard

32.text: rapping at the outer entrance of the house, some twenty feet from the inner

33.text: room. When the entrance was opened, the shaman would appear, quite

34.text: naked, with the drum in his hand.

35.text: At first, on hearing this account, I was disposed to ascribe it to the

36.text: imagination of my Eskimo friends; but, after having seen the legerdemain

37.text: practised by Uˊpuñe and her children, I came to the conclusion that the

38.text: words of my Eskimo informants might have been nearer to the truth than I

39.text: supposed. Indeed, the house of the shaman could have had an underground

40.text: passage similar to the cellars which are sometimes dug under the houses and

41.text: tents, and the shaman might have passed through it to the outside.
